subtitle: The granddaddy of all distortion effects. Vintage fuzz creates a buzzy, saturated tone that defined psychedelic rock and early heavy music.

introduction.title: What is Fuzz?
introduction.text: Fuzz was one of the first guitar effects ever created, originally discovered as a happy accident in broken or overdriven equipment. It creates extreme saturation and compression, turning your guitar signal into a square wave with a distinctive buzzy, aggressive character.

columns.title: Characteristics
columns.text: Extreme signal compression. Square wave clipping. Buzzy, saturated texture. Vintage, lo-fi character. Octave harmonics generation. Sustain and feedback potential.

columns.title: Musical Applications
columns.text: Psychedelic and garage rock. Vintage blues and R&B. Alternative and indie rock. Experimental and noise music. Retro and vintage sounds. Lead guitar textures.

cards.title: 1960: The First Fuzz
cards.description: Producer Joe Meek accidentally created fuzz when a mixing console malfunctioned during a recording session, creating a distorted sound that would inspire a revolution.

cards.title: 1962: "The 2000 Pound Bee"
cards.description: The Tornados' instrumental hit featured one of the first intentional uses of fuzz, created using a faulty channel on Joe Meek's mixing desk.

cards.title: 1965: "(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction"
cards.description: Keith Richards' iconic riff, played through a Maestro Fuzz-Tone, brought fuzz to mainstream rock and launched the pedal industry.

cards.title: Late 1960s: Psychedelic Era
cards.description: Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton, and Jeff Beck elevated fuzz to an art form, using it for feedback, sustain, and otherworldly textures.

cards.title: Germanium Fuzz
cards.description: The original fuzz sound using vintage germanium transistors. Warm, musical, and temperature-sensitive. Classic 1960s character.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Fuzz Face, Tone Bender, Germanium Big Muff

cards.title: Silicon Fuzz
cards.description: More stable and aggressive than germanium. Brighter, more consistent, and better for modern applications.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Silicon Fuzz Face, modern Big Muff variants

cards.title: Op-Amp Fuzz
cards.description: Uses op-amp chips for consistent, high-gain fuzz. Often more versatile with better EQ control and output consistency.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Big Muff Pi, Rat (fuzz mode), modern boutique fuzzes

cards.title: Octave Fuzz
cards.description: Adds octave harmonics to the fuzz signal, creating synth-like textures. Popular in funk and experimental music.

fields.label: Examples
fields.value: Octavia, Roger Mayer Octavia, modern octave fuzzes

cards.title: Dallas Arbiter Fuzz Face
cards.description: The most iconic fuzz pedal ever made. Simple two-knob design with massive personality. Jimi Hendrix's weapon of choice for creating legendary tones.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Warm, musical fuzz that cleans up with guitar volume. Responds to playing dynamics.

cards.title: Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi
cards.description: The sustain king. Thick, woolly fuzz with incredible sustain and a distinctive mid-scooped character. Essential for alternative and indie rock.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Thick, sustaining fuzz with scooped mids and powerful low-end presence

items: J Mascis - Dinosaur Jr. walls of sound
Jack White - White Stripes garage rock

cards.title: Maestro Fuzz-Tone FZ-1
cards.description: The first commercially available fuzz pedal. Made famous by Keith Richards on "Satisfaction." Simple, aggressive, and historically significant.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Raw, buzzy fuzz with simple on/off operation. Pure vintage character.

cards.title: Roger Mayer Octavia
cards.description: Combines fuzz with octave-up generation, creating synth-like textures. Hendrix used it for some of his most otherworldly sounds.

fields.label: Signature Sound
fields.value: Fuzz with upper octave harmonics, creating bell-like and synth-like tones

cards.title: Playing Techniques
items: Single notes work better than chords
Control feedback with distance from amp

cards.title: Signal Chain Tips
items: Wah pedal works great with fuzz

cards.title: Germanium Transistors
items: Temperature sensitive - warm up time needed
Vintage units may need transistor replacement

sections.title: Fuzz Settings Guide
sections.warningText: Fuzz sounds best when it's the star of the show. Use it sparingly in arrangements and give it space to breathe. The guitar volume knob is your best friend for controlling fuzz intensity.
